title: Passing & Movement Challenge
description: Show your soccer passing and movement skills!

questions.question: Your teammate runs into a clear lane ahead. Where should you aim the pass?
options: Into their path with a speed they can reach
Behind them so they must stop
At the position they have already left
As far ahead as you can kick it
questions.explanation: Lead a moving teammate into space. For a stationary or tightly marked player, a pass to feet may be better.

questions.question: What's the best way to make sure your pass reaches your teammate?
options: Look down only at your feet
Call for the ball without scanning
Look at your teammate before passing
Pass before checking pressure
questions.explanation: Always look up to find your teammate before passing.

questions.question: After passing, how can you support the next player?
options: Move to a useful new passing angle
Always follow the ball into the same lane
Stop until the ball is returned
Run forward even when support behind is needed
questions.explanation: Move to help the next action. That may mean going ahead, sideways, or behind, not simply following your pass.

questions.question: What makes a 'give-and-go' work?
options: Pass, move past a defender, and receive a return pass
Pass and wait in the same place for a return
Dribble in a circle before passing
Pass long and stop supporting
questions.explanation: The passer moves into a new lane after releasing the ball. The return pass then helps them get past the defender.

questions.question: If your teammate is covered closely, how can you help them?
options: Stay hidden behind a defender
Stand still on the same line
Move to space so they can pass easier
Move into the defender's cover shadow
questions.explanation: Finding space makes it easier for teammates to pass safely.

questions.question: Which part of your foot gives the most control for short passes?
options: Toe
Heel
Inside of the foot
Outside edge
questions.explanation: The inside of your foot helps you make accurate, controlled passes.

questions.question: Why should you spread out when your team has the ball?
options: So defenders have to chase more
To get closer together in one lane
To leave the wide channels unused
To reduce passing angles
questions.explanation: Spreading out creates space and makes it harder for defenders to cover everyone.

questions.question: When your teammate passes you the ball, how should you receive it?
options: Kick it away from support
Move away from the passing lane
Use a soft touch to control it
Stop your run too early
questions.explanation: A soft first touch helps you control the ball and get ready to pass again quickly.

questions.question: How can you let your teammate know you want the ball?
options: Wave without moving into space
Call their name clearly
Stay quiet while marked
Hide behind a defender
questions.explanation: Clear communication helps teammates know when and where to pass.

questions.question: Passing backwards is:
options: Always bad
Never useful in build-up
Sometimes a smart choice
Only allowed for defenders
questions.explanation: Passing backwards can help keep possession when forward passes are too risky.

questions.question: When should you use a long pass?
options: To switch play to open teammates
Every time you receive the ball
Only when you are near goal
Never when space is open wide
questions.explanation: Long passes help move the ball quickly to open areas far away.

questions.question: A defender may intercept a slow pass. How should you pass to an open nearby teammate?
options: Firmly enough to beat the defender, but with control
As gently as possible every time
As hard as possible regardless of distance
With the same force for every teammate
questions.explanation: Match the weight of the pass to distance, pressure, and the receiver. Too soft can invite an interception; too hard can be difficult to control.

questions.question: Moving without the ball helps you:
options: Pull teammates out of shape
Create passing options
Move into tighter pressure
Make the field smaller
questions.explanation: Moving off the ball creates new opportunities to receive passes and attack.

questions.question: Before passing, you should always:
options: Call before checking options
Check your shoulders and surroundings
Pass without looking up
Jump before striking the ball
questions.explanation: Looking around helps you see teammates and defenders clearly before making a pass.

questions.question: Why can quick passing and movement help against a settled defense?
options: It can move the ball before defenders close the next lane
It means you never need to look up
It makes every forward pass safe
It replaces the need for good spacing
questions.explanation: Move the ball when a useful option is there. Passing quickly is helpful when the team can keep control and create a better angle.

questions.question: What is a good support angle?
options: Standing where your teammate can see and pass to you
Hiding directly behind a defender
Standing on the same line as the ball
Running away from the passing lane
questions.explanation: A support angle gives the player on the ball a clear passing lane.

questions.question: Why should you check your shoulder before receiving?
options: To know if you can turn or need to pass quickly
To watch the crowd instead of pressure
To slow the play down every time
To avoid supporting the ball
questions.explanation: Scanning before the ball arrives helps you make your next decision faster.

questions.question: When is a one-touch pass useful?
options: When you already know the next pass and pressure is close
When you have not scanned yet
When you want extra touches in pressure
When the ball is out of play
questions.explanation: One-touch passing can beat pressure, but only when you have scanned first.

questions.question: You pass for a give-and-go, but a defender blocks your return run. What should you do?
options: Find another useful space instead of forcing the same run
Run into the defender to keep the plan
Demand the return pass through the blocked lane
Stop supporting because the move did not work
questions.explanation: A combination is an option, not a promise. Read how the defender reacts and find the next way to help.

questions.question: If one side of the field is crowded, what should your team try?
options: Switch the ball to the open side
Force another pass into the crowd
All run into the same channel
Clear it even with open support
questions.explanation: Switching play can find space and make defenders shift across the field.

questions.question: What is the central learning idea in a rondo?
options: Keep possession under pressure by using passing angles, support, and quick decisions
Complete a fixed pattern with exactly four outside players and one defender
Keep every player on a cone and avoid changing positions
Practise shooting at goal after every pass
questions.explanation: A rondo is a possession practice against opponents trying to win the ball. Numbers, spaces, and roles can vary. The point is to read pressure and keep useful connections, not memorize one layout.

questions.question: A coach changes a rondo from one defender to two. What should the players with the ball expect?
options: New pressure and blocked lanes, so support and decisions must adapt
Exactly the same passing choices because the outside shape has not changed
No need to scan because the next pass is predetermined
Every pass must now go between the two defenders
questions.explanation: Another defender changes the available space and timing. Sometimes you can play between defenders; sometimes you should go around them or change your angle.

questions.question: A can pass to B, but not directly to C. B can see C arriving in space. How can they connect?
options: A passes to B, who sets the ball for C to receive facing forward
A forces a pass through the defender toward C
C stands directly behind B in the same passing lane
B holds the ball until C is marked
questions.explanation: This is a third-player combination. The middle player connects a pass that was not available directly. The timing of C's movement matters as much as the first pass.

questions.question: You are closely marked in a possession practice. How can your movement still help?
options: Move to take your marker away and open a lane for someone else
Stay hidden and demand the ball
Run toward the ball so all receivers share one lane
Assume every useful movement must end with you receiving
questions.explanation: A supporting run can create space without receiving the ball. Check whether your movement frees a teammate or blocks their lane.

questions.question: You receive with pressure at your back. A teammate facing forward is free behind the passer. What combination may help?
options: Set the ball to the free supporting player and move to offer again
Turn blindly because the goal is ahead
Take extra touches until the marker commits a foul
Pass toward the closest opponent to make them react
questions.explanation: A short set pass can let a teammate with a better view play forward. The first receiver does not have to turn to help the team progress.
